history.q: The Viking Age is traditionally dated from a raid in 793 on which English monastery?
history.fact: Norse raiders struck the Holy Island of Lindisfarne off Northumberland, shocking scholars across Christian Europe.

history.q: Which king is traditionally credited with first uniting Norway in the late 9th century?
history.fact: Legend says Harald vowed not to cut or comb his hair until he ruled all of Norway, hence his nickname.

history.q: In which year did Norway peacefully dissolve its union with Sweden?
history.fact: In a referendum that August, 368,208 Norwegians voted for dissolution and just 184 against.

history.q: Which country invaded Norway on 9 April 1940?
history.fact: The German cruiser Blücher was sunk in the Oslofjord near Drøbak, buying time for the King and government to escape.

history.q: Which Norwegian explorer led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in December 1911?
history.fact: His team reached the pole on 14 December 1911, about five weeks before Robert Falcon Scott's party.

history.q: Norway's National Day, 17 May, commemorates the signing of what in 1814?
choices: The end of the Black Death
history.fact: Children's parades, rather than military ones, are the heart of the day's celebrations across the country.

history.q: German merchants of the Hanseatic League ran a major trading post at the Bryggen wharf in which city?
history.fact: The Hansa traded grain for dried cod from the north; Bryggen's wooden wharf buildings are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.q: For about four centuries until 1814, Norway was ruled in a union from which capital?
history.fact: The union with Denmark began in 1380 under a shared king; Norway's institutions were increasingly run from Copenhagen.

history.q: Which Norwegian politician's surname became a byword for 'traitor' after he collaborated with the Nazi occupiers?
history.fact: He was tried and executed in October 1945, and 'quisling' entered English as a word for a collaborator.

history.q: Which Norwegian king was killed at the Battle of Stamford Bridge in England in 1066?
history.fact: His defeat by Harold Godwinson is often seen as the end of the Viking Age; weeks later Harold lost at Hastings.

history.q: Which king, later Norway's patron saint, died at the Battle of Stiklestad in 1030?
history.fact: His shrine in Trondheim became one of northern Europe's great pilgrimage destinations.

history.q: Under the 1814 Treaty of Kiel, Denmark ceded Norway to which country?
history.fact: Norwegians resisted by drafting their own constitution, and later accepted a union with Sweden that kept it in place.

history.q: Which Danish prince became King Haakon VII of Norway in 1905?
history.fact: Carl asked for a referendum before accepting, and about 79% of voters approved keeping a monarchy.

history.q: In 1943, Norwegian commandos sabotaged the Vemork plant, which was producing what for Nazi Germany?
history.fact: Operation Gunnerside's team escaped without firing a shot; the story inspired the 1965 film 'The Heroes of Telemark'.

history.q: Which explorer let his ship freeze into the Arctic pack ice in 1893 to drift towards the North Pole?
history.fact: Leaving the ship with Hjalmar Johansen, he reached a record 86°14′N on skis before wintering in a stone hut.

history.q: Which union of 1397 brought Norway, Denmark and Sweden under a single monarch?
history.fact: The union was formed at the Swedish castle town of Kalmar; Sweden finally broke away in 1523.

history.q: During the Second World War, what was the 'Shetland Bus'?
choices: Boats ferrying agents and refugees between Shetland and Norway
history.fact: Norwegian fishing boats, and later fast submarine chasers, made the dangerous North Sea crossings, often in winter darkness.

history.q: Oslo was officially known by which name from 1624 until 1925?
history.fact: King Christian IV rebuilt the city after a great fire in 1624 and named it after himself.

history.q: The Black Death reached Norway in 1349 aboard a ship that docked at which port?
history.fact: The plague may have killed around half of the population, leaving many farms abandoned for generations.

history.q: Which Danish prince was elected King of Norway at Eidsvoll in May 1814, but abdicated that October?
history.fact: Christian Frederik later became King Christian VIII of Denmark, ruling from 1839 to 1848.

history.q: The Battle of Hafrsfjord, traditionally linked to Norway's unification, was fought near which modern city?
history.fact: The monument 'Swords in Rock', three giant bronze swords planted in the ground, marks the battle site.

history.q: By what name was Trondheim known in the Middle Ages?
history.fact: Nidaros became the seat of Norway's archbishop in the 1150s, and its great cathedral still stands over St Olaf's burial place.

history.q: Under King Haakon IV, which island accepted Norwegian rule in 1262-64?
history.fact: At its height, the Norwegian realm also included Greenland, the Faroes, Orkney and Shetland.

history.q: By the Treaty of Perth in 1266, Norway ceded the Hebrides and the Isle of Man to which kingdom?
history.fact: The treaty followed the inconclusive Battle of Largs in 1263; Norway kept Orkney and Shetland for two more centuries.

history.q: Which 1814 agreement ended the brief war between Norway and Sweden while preserving Norway's new constitution?
history.fact: Signed in August 1814, it led Christian Frederik to abdicate and Norway to enter a union with Sweden as a separate state.

technology.q: What did Norway discover at the Ekofisk field in the North Sea in 1969?
technology.fact: The discovery turned Norway into one of the world's major exporters of oil and gas.

technology.q: Thor Heyerdahl's 1947 Kon-Tiki raft, which sailed from Peru to Polynesia, was built mainly from which wood?
technology.fact: The crew of six drifted across the Pacific for 101 days; the raft is now displayed at the Kon-Tiki Museum in Oslo.

technology.q: What supplies the vast majority of Norway's electricity?
technology.fact: Rain and snowmelt from the mountains feed well over a thousand hydropower plants.

technology.q: Which kitchen tool did Norwegian carpenter Thor Bjørklund patent in 1925?
technology.fact: Bjørklund's 'ostehøvel' (cheese plane) was inspired by his carpenter's plane and is still made by the family firm in Lillehammer.

technology.q: Which Norwegian tunnel became the world's longest road tunnel when it opened in 2000?
technology.fact: The 24.5 km tunnel has three large caverns lit in blue and yellow to break the monotony and keep drivers alert.

technology.q: Norway is the world's largest producer of which farmed fish?
technology.fact: Norway produces around half of the world's farmed Atlantic salmon, raised in sea pens along its sheltered fjords.

technology.q: In 2018, Norway's state-controlled oil company Statoil changed its name to what?
technology.fact: The new name combines 'equi', for equality and equilibrium, with 'nor', for Norway.

technology.q: Which famous wooden polar ship, used by both Nansen and Amundsen, is displayed in its own museum in Oslo?
technology.fact: Fram is said to have sailed farther north and farther south than any other wooden ship.

technology.q: What does the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, opened in 2008, store deep inside a mountain?
technology.fact: Built near Longyearbyen, the vault can hold millions of seed samples kept frozen at about -18°C.

technology.q: Kristian Birkeland and Sam Eyde developed an electric-arc process to make what, leading to the founding of Norsk Hydro?
technology.fact: Birkeland also explained the aurora as charged particles from the Sun guided by Earth's magnetic field.

technology.q: Troll A, among the tallest structures ever moved by humans, is what kind of installation?
technology.fact: Standing 472 m tall, the concrete platform was towed out to the Troll field in the North Sea in 1995.

technology.q: Equinor's Hywind project pioneered which renewable energy technology?
technology.fact: The first full-scale Hywind test turbine began operating off the island of Karmøy in 2009.

technology.q: Which Norwegian mathematician gave his name to a prize often called the 'Nobel of mathematics'?
technology.fact: Abel proved in 1824 that the general quintic equation cannot be solved by radicals; he died aged just 26.

technology.q: May-Britt and Edvard Moser shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering what?
choices: Grid cells, part of the brain's positioning system
technology.fact: Working in Trondheim, the couple showed how grid cells help the brain map where we are, like an inner GPS.

technology.q: Norwegian engineer Erik Rotheim patented which everyday invention in the 1920s?
technology.fact: In 1998, Norway's postal service marked the invention with a stamp showing an aerosol can.

technology.q: The UNESCO-listed mining town of Røros grew up around the extraction of which metal?
technology.fact: Mining began in 1644 and lasted 333 years; the town's wooden houses survive in remarkably intact streets.

technology.q: Which web browser began as a research project at the Norwegian telecom company Telenor?
technology.fact: Opera Software was spun off in Oslo in 1995 and introduced features such as tabbed browsing and speed dial early on.

technology.q: What is the purpose of the giant mirrors installed above the town of Rjukan in 2013?
choices: Reflecting sunlight into the shaded valley in winter
technology.fact: The deep valley gets no direct sun for about half the year, so computer-steered mirrors beam it onto the town square.

technology.q: Which Norwegian mathematician developed the theory of continuous symmetry groups that now bear his name?
technology.fact: Lie groups underpin modern physics, from particle theory to the mathematics behind relativity.

technology.q: Which Norwegian-born physicist shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on tunnelling in superconductors?
technology.fact: Giaever trained as a mechanical engineer before moving into physics at General Electric in the United States.

technology.q: Which Norwegian whaler patented the explosive harpoon gun in 1870, transforming modern whaling?
technology.fact: Foyn from Tønsberg combined the gun with steam-powered catcher boats, allowing fast rorqual whales to be hunted.

technology.q: The mining town of Kongsberg was founded in 1624 to exploit deposits of which metal?
technology.fact: Kongsberg's silver mines were among the largest industrial sites in Denmark-Norway and operated until 1958.

technology.q: Which pioneering object-oriented programming language was created in Oslo in the 1960s?
technology.fact: Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard received the 2001 Turing Award for Simula, which inspired C++ and Java.

technology.q: Which US company discovered the Ekofisk oil field in 1969?
technology.fact: The find came just before Christmas 1969, after a long run of dry wells had almost ended the search.

technology.q: Ragnar Frisch, co-winner of the first Nobel economics prize in 1969, coined which term?
technology.fact: Frisch shared the prize with Dutch economist Jan Tinbergen for building mathematical models of the economy.

art.q: Which Norwegian artist painted 'The Scream'?
art.fact: Munch made several versions in paint, pastel and print; he said the image came from a sunset walk near Oslo.

art.q: Which composer wrote 'In the Hall of the Mountain King'?
art.fact: Grieg's home, Troldhaugen, near Bergen, is now a museum with a concert hall overlooking a lake.

art.q: Which Henrik Ibsen play ends with Nora slamming the door on her husband and family?
art.fact: First staged in 1879, it caused a sensation; that final door slam was called 'the door slam heard around the world'.

art.q: What are Norway's medieval wooden churches, built with load-bearing posts, called?
art.fact: About 28 survive in Norway, many decorated with dragon heads and carvings that echo Viking art.

art.q: What can visitors famously do on the roof of the Oslo Opera House?
choices: Walk up its sloping marble surface
art.fact: Clad in white Italian marble, the roof rises from the fjord like a glacier and is free to walk on.

art.q: Which Norwegian band had a worldwide hit in 1985 with 'Take On Me'?
art.fact: Its pencil-sketch animated video won six MTV Video Music Awards in 1986.

art.q: Oslo's Frogner Park displays more than 200 sculptures by which artist?
art.fact: Its centrepiece, the Monolith, is carved from a single block of granite with 121 intertwined human figures.

art.q: The kingdom of Arendelle in which Disney film drew inspiration from Norwegian scenery and architecture?
art.fact: Disney artists visited Norway; stave churches, fjords and Bergen's Bryggen all shaped the film's look.

art.q: Which 1991 novel by Jostein Gaarder, an introduction to the history of philosophy, became a worldwide bestseller?
art.fact: It follows a 14-year-old girl who starts receiving mysterious letters asking 'Who are you?'

art.q: Which Norwegian architecture firm designed the Oslo Opera House?
art.fact: Snøhetta, named after a Norwegian mountain, also designed the Bibliotheca Alexandrina in Egypt.

art.q: Which Norwegian author of the novel 'Hunger' won the 1920 Nobel Prize in Literature?
art.fact: 'Hunger' (1890), about a starving young writer in Christiania, is often seen as a forerunner of modernist fiction.

art.q: Which writer won the 1928 Nobel Prize in Literature, notably for the medieval trilogy 'Kristin Lavransdatter'?
art.fact: Undset's home, Bjerkebæk in Lillehammer, is now a museum.

art.q: Who wrote the words of Norway's national anthem, 'Ja, vi elsker dette landet'?
art.fact: Bjørnson won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Literature; the anthem's melody is by his cousin Rikard Nordraak.

art.q: Which Norwegian folk instrument has extra sympathetic strings running beneath the ones that are bowed?
art.fact: Hardanger fiddles are often richly decorated with mother-of-pearl inlay and a carved dragon or lion head.

art.q: Edvard Grieg's 'Peer Gynt' music was written for a play by which dramatist?
art.fact: The play premiered in Christiania in 1876; Grieg later arranged his music into two popular orchestral suites.

art.q: A version of 'The Scream' was stolen from Oslo's National Gallery in 1994 on the opening day of which event?
art.fact: The thieves left a note thanking the gallery for its poor security; the painting was recovered undamaged months later.

art.q: Which Norwegian actress starred in Ingmar Bergman films such as 'Persona' and 'Scenes from a Marriage'?
art.fact: Ullmann later directed films herself, including 'Faithless' (2000), from a script by Bergman.

art.q: Rosemaling is a traditional Norwegian style of what?
art.fact: Flowing flowers and scrolls in rosemaling decorated rural chests, bowls and church walls, especially from the 1700s.

art.q: The richly decorated Oseberg ship, buried around 834 CE, was the grave of whom?
choices: A Viking chieftain and his sons
art.fact: The burial included a carved cart, sledges, beds and animals; the ship is the finest surviving Viking vessel.

art.q: Which Norwegian stave church, famous for its animal carvings, is on the UNESCO World Heritage List?
art.fact: Its carvings of interlaced beasts gave their name to the 'Urnes style', the last phase of Viking art.

art.q: Munch grouped 'The Scream' with works such as 'Madonna' and 'The Dance of Life' in a series he called what?
art.fact: The series explored love, anxiety and death, themes Munch called 'a poem about life'.

art.q: Which painter's 'Winter Night in the Mountains' was voted Norway's national painting in a 1995 poll?
art.fact: Sohlberg was inspired by the snow-covered Rondane mountains seen under a deep blue winter sky.

art.q: Which 19th-century painter is often called the father of Norwegian landscape painting?
art.fact: Dahl spent most of his career in Dresden but returned to paint Norway's mountains, fjords and stave churches.

art.q: Edvard Grieg's only completed piano concerto is in which key?
art.fact: Grieg wrote it at 24, and its dramatic opening flourish is one of the best-known in classical music.

art.q: Which two painters created the 1848 painting 'Bridal Procession on the Hardangerfjord' together?
choices: J. C. Dahl and Thomas Fearnley
art.fact: Gude painted the landscape and Tidemand the people; the work became an icon of National Romanticism.

politics.q: What is the capital of Norway?
politics.fact: Oslo sits at the head of the Oslofjord, and more than half of its area is forest and protected nature.

politics.q: In which city is the Nobel Peace Prize awarded each year?
politics.fact: Alfred Nobel's will gave the Peace Prize to a committee chosen by Norway's parliament; the other prizes are awarded in Stockholm.

politics.q: What is the name of Norway's parliament?
politics.fact: The name roughly means 'the great assembly' and echoes the 'things', or assemblies, of Viking times.

politics.q: Who became King of Norway in 1991?
politics.fact: Born in 1937, Harald was the first king born in Norway in more than 500 years; he sailed for Norway at the Olympics.

politics.q: In referendums held in 1972 and 1994, Norwegian voters rejected joining which organisation?
politics.fact: The 1994 vote was close: about 52% voted no.

politics.q: Norway was a founding member of which military alliance in 1949?
politics.fact: Norway was the only founding member to share a border with the Soviet Union.

politics.q: Who became Norway's first female Prime Minister, in 1981?
politics.fact: In 1986 she formed a cabinet in which 8 of 18 ministers were women, then a world record.

politics.q: Norway's huge sovereign wealth fund was built mainly from revenue from what?
politics.fact: Officially the Government Pension Fund Global, it invests abroad and owns roughly 1.5% of all listed shares in the world.

politics.q: Which Norwegian became the first Secretary-General of the United Nations, in 1946?
politics.fact: Lie had been Norway's foreign minister in exile in London during the Second World War.

politics.q: At which manor house was Norway's constitution drafted and signed in 1814?
politics.fact: The 112 representatives became known as the 'Eidsvoll men'; the building is now a national museum.

politics.q: In which year did Norwegian women gain the vote in national elections on equal terms with men?
politics.fact: Norway was one of the first independent countries to do so; women's rights pioneer Gina Krog campaigned for decades.

politics.q: The 1993 Oslo Accords, prepared in secret talks hosted by Norway, were agreements between Israel and whom?
politics.fact: The first accord was signed on the White House lawn in Washington in September 1993.

politics.q: The Sámi Parliament of Norway, opened in 1989, sits in which northern town?
politics.fact: Its building is shaped to evoke a lavvu, the traditional Sámi tent.

politics.q: What was the 'Nansen passport', introduced in 1922?
choices: An identity document for stateless refugees
A League of Nations diplomatic passport
politics.fact: Fridtjof Nansen won the 1922 Nobel Peace Prize for his work helping refugees and prisoners of war.

politics.q: Which former Norwegian Prime Minister served as NATO Secretary General from 2014 to 2024?
politics.fact: He became one of NATO's longest-serving Secretaries General, second only to Joseph Luns.

politics.q: How many members sit in the Storting?
politics.fact: Members are elected for fixed four-year terms by proportional representation from the counties.

politics.q: Gro Harlem Brundtland chaired a UN commission whose 1987 report popularised which concept?
politics.fact: The report 'Our Common Future' defined it as meeting present needs without compromising those of future generations.

politics.q: Through which agreement does Norway take part in the EU's single market without being an EU member?
politics.fact: The EEA came into force in 1994 and links the EU with Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

politics.q: Who was Norway's Prime Minister when the union with Sweden was dissolved in 1905?
politics.fact: Michelsen, a Bergen shipowner, led the government that steered the peaceful break from Sweden.

politics.q: Which is the only country with an older single-document national constitution still in force than Norway's?
politics.fact: Norway's constitution of 17 May 1814 drew inspiration from the US Constitution and French revolutionary ideas.

politics.q: The 1920 Svalbard Treaty recognised Norway's sovereignty while giving signatories' citizens what?
choices: The right to build military bases
Equal rights to economic activity such as mining
Shared ownership of the islands' land
Free passage to the North Pole
politics.fact: The treaty came into force in 1925, and Russia's coal town of Barentsburg operates under its terms.

politics.q: What is unusual about Norway's parliament compared with most parliamentary democracies?
choices: Its members are chosen by lottery
It cannot be dissolved for early elections
It meets only once every two years
politics.fact: Elections are held every four years without exception, so governments must find majorities within each term.

politics.q: What is the royal motto of Norway, first adopted by King Haakon VII?
politics.fact: 'All for Norway' became a rallying cry during the Second World War, when the King led resistance from exile.

politics.q: Which Labour Prime Minister, often called the 'father of the nation', led Norway's post-war rebuilding?
politics.fact: Gerhardsen, a former road worker who survived a concentration camp, served as Prime Minister for about 17 years in total.

politics.q: Who was the Labour Prime Minister heading Norway's government-in-exile in London during the Second World War?
politics.fact: His government had fled with King Haakon VII in June 1940 and returned to Norway after liberation in 1945.

current-affairs.q: Which Norwegian writer won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2023?
current-affairs.fact: The Swedish Academy praised Fosse's plays and prose for 'giving voice to the unsayable'; he writes in Nynorsk.

current-affairs.q: In October 2021, a new 13-storey museum devoted to which artist opened on Oslo's waterfront?
current-affairs.fact: The tower holds tens of thousands of works that Munch bequeathed to the city of Oslo.

current-affairs.q: In 2024, roughly what share of new cars sold in Norway were fully electric?
current-affairs.fact: Tax breaks, toll discounts and dense charging networks made Norway the world leader in switching to electric cars.

current-affairs.q: Norway topped the medal table at the 2022 Winter Olympics, hosted by which city?
current-affairs.fact: Norway won 16 gold medals, a record for a single Winter Games at the time.

current-affairs.q: Which Norwegian striker set a Premier League record of 36 goals in the 2022-23 season?
current-affairs.fact: Haaland, born in Leeds, scored his goals for Manchester City as they won the treble that season.

current-affairs.q: At the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, Karsten Warholm won gold and set a world record in which event?
current-affairs.fact: Warholm ran 45.94 seconds, the first time anyone had broken 46 seconds in the event.

current-affairs.q: Who became Norway's Prime Minister in October 2021?
current-affairs.fact: The Labour leader took over from Conservative Erna Solberg after the September 2021 election.

current-affairs.q: At the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, Jakob Ingebrigtsen won gold in which event?
current-affairs.fact: He set an Olympic record of 3:28.32, and later won 5000 m gold at the Paris Games in 2024.

current-affairs.q: Norway's women won Olympic gold in which team sport at the Paris 2024 Games?
current-affairs.fact: They beat hosts France 29-21 in the final in Lille.

current-affairs.q: In February 2025, former NATO chief Jens Stoltenberg returned to Norwegian government in which role?
current-affairs.fact: He joined Jonas Gahr Støre's cabinet after the Centre Party left the coalition.

current-affairs.q: Which Norwegian tennis player reached the men's singles final at the French Open in both 2022 and 2023?
current-affairs.fact: He lost to Rafael Nadal in 2022 and to Novak Djokovic in 2023; his father Christian was also a tour player.

current-affairs.q: In 2023, which player won the world chess title that Magnus Carlsen had chosen not to defend?
current-affairs.fact: Carlsen had held the classical title since 2013 and said he lacked motivation to play another match.

current-affairs.q: Which party won the most seats in Norway's parliamentary election of September 2025?
current-affairs.fact: The result kept Jonas Gahr Støre in office as Prime Minister.

current-affairs.q: In 2022, Norway overtook which country to become the largest supplier of natural gas to the European Union?
current-affairs.fact: Norwegian gas flows through a network of subsea pipelines thousands of kilometres long to Germany, Britain and beyond.

current-affairs.q: Which giant North Sea oil field, named after a 19th-century prime minister, began production in October 2019?
current-affairs.fact: The field is powered by electricity from shore, giving it some of the lowest production emissions in the industry.

current-affairs.q: In June 2022, Oslo opened a new building for which institution, the largest art museum in the Nordic countries?
current-affairs.fact: Its rooftop 'Light Hall' glows at night and is used for large temporary exhibitions.

current-affairs.q: Which member of Norway's royal family turned 18 in January 2022?
current-affairs.fact: She is second in line to the throne, after her father, Crown Prince Haakon.

current-affairs.q: Which Arctic Norwegian city was a European Capital of Culture in 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Bodø was the first European Capital of Culture north of the Arctic Circle.

current-affairs.q: Hywind Tampen, the floating wind farm opened in the North Sea in 2023, was built to power what?
current-affairs.fact: Its 11 turbines supply electricity to the Snorre and Gullfaks fields, cutting their use of gas turbines.

current-affairs.q: In 2024, Norway partly reversed a 2020 reform, raising its number of counties from 11 to how many?
current-affairs.fact: Several merged counties, such as Viken and Troms og Finnmark, were split up again from 1 January 2024.

current-affairs.q: Which Oslo library, opened in 2020, was named the world's Public Library of the Year in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Its cantilevered upper floors and light-filled central atrium stand beside the Oslo Opera House in Bjørvika.

current-affairs.q: In August 2024, Princess Märtha Louise held her wedding in which famous fjord village?
current-affairs.fact: She married American Durek Verrett at the Hotel Union in Geiranger, beside the UNESCO-listed fjord.

current-affairs.q: Which Japanese organisation of atomic-bomb survivors received the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo in December 2024?
current-affairs.fact: The Norwegian Nobel Committee honoured its decades of testimony by 'hibakusha', survivors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

current-affairs.q: At the 2025 Nordic World Ski Championships in Trondheim, how many gold medals did Johannes Høsflot Klæbo win?
current-affairs.fact: Racing on home snow, the Trondheim skier won every men's cross-country event on the programme.

current-affairs.q: Which Norwegian city held the title of European Green Capital in 2019?
current-affairs.fact: The city had reopened buried streams, restricted cars in the centre and expanded electric public transport.

society.q: By the end of 2024, Norway's Government Pension Fund Global, the oil fund, was worth closest to how much?
society.fact: That works out at over 300,000 US dollars for every Norwegian; the fund owns about 1.5% of all listed shares in the world.

society.q: Most of Norway's electricity comes from which source?
society.fact: Hydropower supplies roughly 90% of generation, which is why the 2021-22 price surge in the south came as a shock to households.

society.q: What is Norway's standard rate of VAT?
society.fact: Food is taxed at a reduced 15%, and transport, cinema and hotel stays at 12%, which still leaves Norway with some of Europe's highest shop prices.

society.q: In December 2021, Norway introduced a scheme paying part of households' bills for what?
society.fact: The 'strømstøtte' covers a share of the price above a set threshold per kilowatt-hour and was extended repeatedly as prices stayed high.

society.q: Since 2022, people from which country have made up by far the largest group of refugees arriving in Norway?
society.fact: More than 80,000 Ukrainians had been granted collective protection by 2024, the largest refugee arrival in Norway's history.

society.q: In Norway, wine and spirits can be bought only from which state-owned chain?
society.fact: Supermarkets may sell drinks up to 4.7% alcohol, and only until 8pm on weekdays; high prices send many Norwegians over the border to Sweden.

society.q: What is the standard age at which Norwegians draw the full state pension?
society.fact: The pension can be drawn flexibly from 62 to 75, with higher monthly payments for those who wait longer.

society.q: Norway's unemployment rate in 2024, as measured by the labour force survey, was closest to which figure?
society.fact: Unemployment stayed low after the pandemic, while employers in care, construction and hospitality reported shortages of workers.

society.q: What statutory national minimum wage does Norway have?
society.fact: Pay is set by collective agreements, though minimum rates in sectors such as cleaning and construction are made legally binding for everyone.

society.q: In 2023, Norway's population passed which milestone?
society.fact: Growth came almost entirely from immigration, with Ukrainian arrivals pushing 2022 and 2023 to record net migration.

society.q: Norges Bank raised its policy interest rate from zero in 2021 to a peak of what in December 2023?
society.fact: The rate stayed at 4.5% for a year and a half before the first cut in June 2025, squeezing households with floating-rate mortgages.

society.q: Norway's consumer price inflation peaked in October 2022 at closest to which figure?
society.fact: It was the highest reading since the late 1980s, driven by electricity, food and a weak krone that made imports dearer.

society.q: In 2022, billionaire Kjell Inge Røkke moved from Norway to which country, highlighting a trend among wealthy Norwegians?
society.fact: Dozens of rich Norwegians relocated after increases in the wealth tax, prompting a public debate about the tax's design.

society.q: In Norway's 2019 local elections, a new protest party won seats by campaigning against which charges on motorists?
society.fact: The 'People's Action No to More Road Tolls' took about 17% of the vote in Bergen, where toll rings fund roads and public transport.

society.q: Norwegian employees on sick leave receive what share of their normal salary for up to a year?
society.fact: Employers pay the first 16 days and the state the rest; Norway's sickness absence rate is among the highest in the OECD.

society.q: At full pay, how many weeks of paid parental leave do Norwegian parents share after a birth?
society.fact: Parents can instead take 59 weeks at 80% pay; 15 weeks are reserved for each parent so that fathers take their share.

society.q: In September 2022, a months-long strike by which group in Norway was ended by government-imposed compulsory arbitration?
society.fact: The strike had kept thousands of pupils out of class since the start of the school year; the government cited harm to pupils' mental health.

society.q: From autumn 2023, Norway began charging university tuition fees to students from where?
society.fact: Higher education had been free for everyone; the change led to a sharp fall in new students from countries such as China, India and Nepal.

society.q: Norway's total fertility rate fell to a record low of about what in 2023?
society.fact: The rate was 1.98 in 2009; the government appointed a birth-rate committee in 2024 to look into the causes of the decline.

society.q: Norway's fiscal rule limits the government's annual spending of oil fund money to about what share of the fund's value?
society.fact: The limit was cut from 4% to 3% in 2017 as expected returns fell; it still covers roughly a fifth of the state budget.

society.q: From August 2024, the maximum monthly price of a kindergarten place in Norway was cut to how many kroner?
society.fact: The cap had been 3,000 kroner; places are free for the third child and in parts of northern Norway.

society.q: Which is the largest of the three groups that dominate Norway's grocery market?
society.fact: NorgesGruppen, owner of Kiwi and Meny, held over 40% of the market; the competition authority fined the big three in 2024 over price-scanning data.

society.q: From 2023, Norway charged VAT on the part of an electric car's price above how many kroner?
society.fact: It was the first dent in the full VAT exemption that had made electric cars cheaper than petrol equivalents for over a decade.

society.q: In 2019, couriers for which food-delivery company held a five-week strike in Norway that won them a collective agreement?
society.fact: It was seen as the first successful strike in Norway's gig economy; the couriers were employees rather than freelancers.

society.q: In 2023, Norway's parliament agreed to extend its 40% gender quota for company boards to which firms?
society.fact: The quota had applied to listed companies since 2008; the extension is being phased in from 2024 for firms with over 100 employees or 100 million kroner in revenue.

general.q: Norway's coast is famous for which deep, narrow sea inlets carved by glaciers?
general.fact: Counting all its fjords and islands, Norway's coastline is over 100,000 km long.

general.q: Which natural light display can often be seen over Tromsø on clear winter nights?
general.fact: Tromsø lies inside the auroral oval, making it one of the best places on Earth to see the aurora borealis.

general.q: What is Norway's currency?
general.fact: Norway introduced the krone in 1875, as part of a Scandinavian monetary union with Denmark and Sweden.

general.q: Brunost, a Norwegian favourite, is what kind of food?
general.fact: Its sweet flavour comes from boiling whey until the milk sugars caramelise; it is sliced thinly with a cheese slicer.

general.q: Through the 2022 Games, which country had won the most medals in Winter Olympics history?
general.fact: Much of Norway's success has come in cross-country skiing, biathlon and speed skating.

general.q: Oslo's Holmenkollen is famous for what kind of winter sports venue?
general.fact: Ski jumping has been held at Holmenkollen since 1892, and the hill was rebuilt in a sleek modern form for 2011.

general.q: Which Indigenous people traditionally live across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia's Kola Peninsula?
general.fact: Reindeer herding remains an important part of Sámi culture, and Sámi National Day is celebrated on 6 February.

general.q: Which clifftop in Finnmark is famously promoted as the northern tip of Europe?
general.fact: North Cape is actually on the island of Magerøya; the mainland's northernmost point is Kinnarodden.

general.q: Which city, surrounded by seven mountains, is Norway's second largest?
general.fact: Bergen is one of Europe's rainiest cities, and locals joke that its children are born with umbrellas.

general.q: What is Norway's longest and deepest fjord?
general.fact: Sognefjord stretches about 200 km inland and reaches a depth of around 1,300 m.

general.q: Preikestolen, the famous flat-topped cliff also called Pulpit Rock, towers over which fjord?
general.fact: Its flat top stands about 604 m above the water, and the hike up draws hundreds of thousands of visitors a year.

general.q: Which two fjords together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in 2005?
general.fact: Waterfalls such as the Seven Sisters tumble down the steep cliffs of Geirangerfjord.

general.q: What are the two official written standards of the Norwegian language?
general.fact: Nynorsk was built by Ivar Aasen in the 1800s from rural dialects; Bokmål grew out of written Danish.

general.q: Which traditional Norwegian Christmas dish is dried whitefish, usually cod, treated with lye?
general.fact: Soaking in lye gives the fish a jelly-like texture; it is often served with bacon, peas and potatoes.

general.q: What is Norway's highest mountain?
general.fact: At about 2,469 m, the peak in the Jotunheimen range is the highest in northern Europe.

general.q: Which Norwegian city hosted the 1952 Winter Olympics?
general.fact: They were the first Winter Games held in a Scandinavian country and the first to feature an Olympic flame relay.

general.q: The Hurtigruten coastal voyage famously runs from Bergen to which town near the Russian border?
general.fact: Founded in 1893 to carry mail and goods, the route calls at more than 30 ports along the coast.

general.q: Which Norwegian cross-country skier won 15 Winter Olympic medals between 2002 and 2018?
general.fact: Eight of her 15 Olympic medals were gold; she retired soon after the 2018 Games in PyeongChang.

general.q: What is Norway's longest river?
general.fact: The Glomma flows about 600 km from near Røros to the Oslofjord at Fredrikstad.

general.q: Saltstraumen, one of the world's strongest tidal currents, is found near which city?
general.fact: Every six hours, hundreds of millions of cubic metres of seawater force through a narrow strait, forming whirlpools.

general.q: Which Ice Age animal was reintroduced to the Dovrefjell mountains in the 20th century?
general.fact: Musk oxen were brought over from Greenland, and today a herd roams Dovrefjell-Sunndalsfjella National Park.

general.q: How is rakfisk, a Norwegian winter speciality, traditionally prepared?
general.fact: Usually made from trout or char, it is eaten raw with flatbread, onions and sour cream, especially around Christmas.

general.q: At the 1998 FIFA World Cup, Norway famously beat which reigning champion 2-1?
general.fact: Kjetil Rekdal's late penalty in Marseille sealed the win and sent Norway through to the knockout stage.

general.q: Sondre Norheim, a pioneer of modern skiing, came from which region that gave its name to a ski technique?
general.fact: Norheim designed skis with curved sides and stiffer bindings, making turns on steep slopes far easier.

general.q: Trolltunga, the 'Troll's Tongue' rock ledge, is usually reached by a long hike from near which town?
general.fact: The ledge juts out about 700 m above Lake Ringedalsvatnet; the return hike takes most of a day.
